payload.coherence_check: One proposal was handed in; there is no second proposal to compose against, and nothing here has been disagreed with by anybody. What I checked was the proposal against the measured record, not against another design. Three checks: (1) the proposal's rejection of the Global\ branch rests entirely on spike 1's result (S4U scheduled-task creation refused by the agent sandbox); re-read the spike record and confirmed the refusal is the sandbox's own policy guard, independent of Windows privilege, and that spikes 2 and 3 never produced a cross-session measurement -- so the proposal is not arguing around a settled 'no', it is accepting one. (2) The proposal's claim that this is materially smaller than a fresh slice matches build-check's own framing verbatim ('no new mutex behaviour, no new test infrastructure -- three doc-comment corrections'), and the three files it targets (StallRig/Program.cs:13, StalledShareTests.cs:17, WindowCases.ps1:1333) are exactly the three build-check named as still stale. (3) Nothing in the six answered questions bears on this slice or contradicts the proposal's choices; the risk tier (low) is correctly left alone because this slice touches no scanner or counting-rule code, only test rig identifiers and comments. The one thing this composition step added beyond the proposal itself: the proposal's own worklist and grep commands are prose promises, not a gate, so I added three narrowly-scoped architecture_rules that turn 'these three files must not say machine-wide again' into something a future build actually fails on, rather than something a future reviewer has to remember to re-grep for by hand.

contracts.name: RigLock scope (RigLock.SessionName / RigLock.Take)
contracts.notes: Behaviour is unchanged and now stated honestly: rig runs in the same sign-in session are serialised (a second run waits, a live holder makes the next run fail loudly, a killed holder does not block -- the existing 18 tests cover this); runs in different sign-in sessions are not serialised, by design, and the mutex string is still `Local\FsAnalyser-SmbRig`, so any process that opens it by string is unaffected by the identifier rename.
contracts.error_cases: Unchanged from SL-038: a live holder leads to a loud failure, an abandoned mutex does not block. Cross-session: no error and no exclusion -- that is the documented scope, not a defect.
contracts.auth_model: Same-user, same-session. The kernel object uses the default DACL from `new Mutex(false, name)`; no MutexSecurity, no NamedWaitHandleOptions.

contracts.name: Slice verification commands
contracts.notes: (1) `pwsh -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File eng/dotnet.ps1 test FsAnalyser.slnx --filter "FullyQualifiedName~SmbRigTests"` still passes 18/18. (2) WindowCases.ps1's Update-StallRig (or an equivalent direct build of tests/window/StallRig through eng/dotnet.ps1) exits 0, proving the rename compiles outside the slnx. (3) Parse tests/window/WindowCases.ps1 with `[System.Management.Automation.Language.Parser]::ParseFile` under both powershell.exe 5.1 and pwsh 7, zero errors. (4) A case-insensitive grep over tests/ and docs/ for machine-wide|on this machine|MachineName returns no hit about RigLock or rig serialisation; any remaining hit about something unrelated (e.g. the SDK bootstrap) is listed and left alone, not bulk-edited.
contracts.error_cases: A missed reference in StallRig fails (2); an encoding break in WindowCases.ps1 fails (3) under 5.1; a leftover claim fails (4).

cross_domain_transfer.source_domain: Single-instance enforcement in desktop apps (Rust win-desktop-utils, .NET NamedWaitHandleOptions)
cross_domain_transfer.pattern: Make the scope of a named kernel object explicit in the identifier or API (CurrentSession vs Global), default to session scope, and treat cross-session as an explicit opt-in that must be proven before it is claimed.
cross_domain_transfer.rationale: Single-instance apps and this test rig's lock use the same Windows mechanism for different ends. Those libraries settled on naming the scope and defaulting to session; that is this slice's resolution too: the scope becomes visible in the constant's name and the docs, and Global\ stays an unproven, explicitly deferred opt-in rather than a claim nobody checked.

invariants.precondition: The name prefix alone decides the scope: a Local\ or unprefixed name is per session, and Global\ spans sessions.
invariants.evidence: Quoted Microsoft docs (cited exchangetuts page) and the cited cross-user-mutex answer; matches SmbRig.cs:176's Local\FsAnalyser-SmbRig with the plain new Mutex(false, name) constructor at SmbRig.cs:186.

invariants.precondition: Nothing runs the SMB rig outside the person's interactive sign-in session.
invariants.evidence: The rig is opt-in via Trait Network=SMB-LOOPBACK, excluded by the default VSTestTestCaseFilter, run by no engine stage. Spikes recorded SessionId=1 for every run performed.

invariants.precondition: Renaming the C# constant leaves the kernel object unchanged: every consumer, C#, PowerShell, or StallRig, still opens Local\FsAnalyser-SmbRig.
invariants.evidence: Grep for MachineName across tests/ (including tests/window) and docs/, then build StallRig separately since it sits outside FsAnalyser.slnx.

invariants.precondition: The rig's mapping sweep sees only its own sign-in session's SMB mappings, so a per-session lock covers everything the sweep can touch.
invariants.evidence: Recalled, not measured on this machine: SMB client connections belong to a logon session. If false, two sessions could interfere and the doc's stated limit would need to say so more strongly, but that is not this slice's defect to fix.

key_decisions.decision: Resolve SL-059 by correcting the claims; RigLock stays Local\ (per sign-in session).
key_decisions.rationale: Switching the prefix is a one-line change, so keeping Local\ today constrains nothing later. SL-038's own design record already chose Local\, and nothing since gives a reason to reverse it: the Global\ spike was blocked before it could measure cross-session exclusion. The rig is opt-in, excluded from every engine stage, and every observed run has been in one interactive session. Of the three build-check criteria, the two marked 'missing' (the Global\ switch and the cross-session test) are the rejected alternative of an either/or slice, not unfinished work; only the third (correcting the claims) is this design's obligation.

key_decisions.decision: Do not build a cross-session test.
key_decisions.rationale: The only unattended route to a second logon session is an S4U scheduled task, and spike 1 showed the agent sandbox refuses to create one because it would change the person's machine settings on every run. A test the loop can never execute is an unexecuted claim, which is the same species of drift this slice exists to close. The trigger for building it later, by hand, is written into the docs instead.

key_decisions.decision: Rename RigLock.MachineName to RigLock.SessionName; leave the string value unchanged.
key_decisions.rationale: The identifier is the one remaining place that claims machine scope that a plain grep for prose phrases cannot catch. This follows the cited pattern of naming scope explicitly (InstanceScope::CurrentSession, NamedWaitHandleOptions.CurrentSessionOnly). Because the string value is untouched, any process opening the lock by name, including an older build of a rig, still contends for the same kernel object; the compiler checks every reference inside FsAnalyser.slnx, and the build-verification step checks StallRig outside it.

key_decisions.decision: Do not edit SL-038's own records under .taad (the builder's account, code-review-2.json).
key_decisions.rationale: Those records are a history of what was claimed and when; rewriting them would hide the drift rather than close it. The live claims are in code and docs, and those are what this slice changes.

key_decisions.decision: Add three narrow architecture_rules over the exact three stale files, rather than one broad glob or none.
key_decisions.rationale: The proposal's own worklist and grep commands are prose promises a future editor can forget to re-run; a glob over the whole tests/window/** or tests/FsAnalyser.Core.Tests/** tree risks matching an unrelated, legitimate use of the phrase elsewhere in those large trees. Scoping to the exact three files the survey and SL-038's own code review already named keeps the rule from ever firing on correct code while still catching a third recurrence of a claim that has already survived one full slice unfixed.

prior_art.pattern: A named mutex with no prefix gets Local\ and is visible only in its own terminal-server session; Global\ is visible in all sessions; names differing only by prefix are separate objects.
The popular accepted fix for a single instance per machine across users is to prefix the mutex name with Global\ -- the bigger, unneeded answer to this slice's title.

A machine-wide mutex made Global\ plus a MutexSecurity rule granting BUILTIN\Users FullControl -- the failure mode to avoid if the lock is ever switched, since any local user could then squat the name and block every rig run.

dotnet/runtime added NamedWaitHandleOptions (CurrentUserOnly, CurrentSessionOnly), both defaulting to true -- the runtime team now treats session- and user-scoping as the safe default and cross-session as an explicit opt-in. Whether this is on the .NET 10 GA surface is recalled, not verified here.
A single-instance helper exposes scope as an explicit enum, InstanceScope::CurrentSession (Local\) vs Global, defaulting to CurrentSession -- the model for renaming MachineName to SessionName.

new Mutex(false, name) on a Global\ name another user already created with the default DACL throws UnauthorizedAccessException instead of waiting -- Global\ alone is cross-session for the same user but fails loudly across different users.
SMB/net-use connections, including New-SmbMapping, belong to a logon session, so a per-session lock matches the reach of the rig's own mapping sweep.
prior_art.where: Windows SMB client / DOS device namespace behaviour

proposals.note: The full resolution -- keep Local\, correct the three remaining stale comments, rename the constant, and write the revisit trigger into the docs -- was adopted essentially unchanged; its rejection of the Global\ branch rests directly on spike 1's result and was verified against that spike record rather than taken on faith. The one addition made in composing this design is turning the proposal's grep-and-build worklist into three enforceable architecture_rules, since prose verification steps are promises a future editor can skip and a regex gate is not.

payload.selection_rationale: The proposal is the only one submitted, and it holds up against every piece of measured reality it touches. It treats spike 1's refusal (the agent sandbox vetoing scheduled-task creation) as decisive rather than an obstacle to route around, which matches this project's own instruction that a verdict from a real experiment outranks reasoning about it. It targets exactly the three files build-check named as still unfixed since SL-038, and no others, avoiding both under-scope (leaving live drift) and over-scope (rewriting unrelated 'on this machine' text about the SDK bootstrap, which the survey's own grep would also catch). It declines to build a cross-session test the loop could never execute, naming that directly as the over-engineering trap the popular prior art (Global\\ + prove it) would walk into -- which is the over_engineering_flag signal this composition step is told to treat as real rather than override with taste. Every change is cheap to reverse (a rename, three comment edits, a doc sentence), matches the low risk tier (no scanner or counting-rule code is touched), and leaves a written trigger so a future slice that does need cross-session exclusion inherits a decision rather than reconstructing the history.
